revealWordProblem.title: Apply: Trophy Case Display
revealWordProblem.text: The school trophy case has 84 trophies to arrange on shelves. The display designer wants to break 84 down into its prime factors first, then use those primes to decide how many equal-sized groups of trophies she can create. What is the prime factorization of 84, written both as a product of primes and using exponents? Show each step of your factor tree.
revealWordProblem.sampleAnswer: 84 = 2 × 42. Since 42 is not prime, split it: 42 = 2 × 21. Since 21 is not prime, split it: 21 = 3 × 7. Both 3 and 7 are prime, so the tree is done. The prime factorization of 84 is 2 × 2 × 3 × 7, which can be written with exponents as 2² × 3 × 7. Check: 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 4 × 3 × 7 = 12 × 7 = 84. Correct.

conceptIntro.heading: Let's build it together — What is prime factorization?
conceptIntro.intro: Prime factorization means writing a number as a product of prime numbers only. A prime number can be divided only by 1 and itself, like 2, 3, 5, and 7. We'll walk through a worked example, try one together, then you'll try a few with hints right there when you need them.
conceptIntro.keyIdea: Keep breaking a number apart until every factor is a prime number you cannot split anymore.

iDo.title: Watch me
lines: I want the prime factorization of 60. I start by splitting it: 60 = 6 × 10.
6 is not prime, so I break it: 6 = 2 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so I stop those branches.
10 is not prime, so I break it: 10 = 2 × 5. Both 2 and 5 are prime, so I stop.
Using exponents, I write it as 2² × 3 × 5. I check: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5 = 60. Correct.

weDo.title: Let's try together
lines: Let's factor 12 together. What is one way to split 12 into two factors? (You might say 3 × 4.)
Is 3 prime? Yes, so we keep it. Is 4 prime? No — what is 4 split apart? (4 = 2 × 2.)
So put the prime factors together: 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. Every factor is prime, so we are done.
Sentence frame — say it with me: "My first step is ___ , because the problem asks for ___ ."

approaching.stem: Which of the following is a prime number?
approaching.explanation: 17 has exactly two factors: 1 and 17. 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7, and 9 = 3 × 3, so they are all composite.
choiceFeedback: 15 = 3 × 5, so it has factors besides 1 and itself. A prime number has exactly two factors — test whether any smaller number divides your choice evenly.
21 breaks apart into 3 × 7, so it has more than two factors. Look for the number that can only be divided by 1 and itself.
9 splits into 3 × 3, which gives it a third factor besides 1 and 9. Keep checking each number for a hidden factor pair.
hints: Re-read what 'prime' means: exactly two factors, 1 and itself. Any extra factor makes a number composite.
Test each choice by dividing by small primes like 2, 3, 5, and 7. If anything divides in evenly, that number is composite.
Start with 9: since 3 × 3 = 9, it has a factor besides 1 and 9, so 9 is composite. Cross it off and test the next choice the same way.
approaching.stemEs: ¿Cuál de los siguientes es un número primo?
approaching.explanationEs: 17 tiene exactamente dos factores: 1 y 17. 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7 y 9 = 3 × 3, así que todos son compuestos.
hintsEs: Relee qué significa 'primo': exactamente dos factores, el 1 y él mismo. Cualquier factor de más vuelve compuesto al número.
Prueba cada opción dividiendo entre primos pequeños como 2, 3, 5 y 7. Si alguno divide exacto, ese número es compuesto.
Empieza con el 9: como 3 × 3 = 9, tiene un factor además del 1 y el 9, así que el 9 es compuesto. Táchalo y prueba la siguiente opción igual.

approaching.stem: What is the prime factorization of 30?
approaching.explanation: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. All three factors (2, 3, 5) are prime, so 2 × 3 × 5 is the prime factorization.
choiceFeedback: That is what you get if you stopped too early — 6 is not prime, it still breaks down into 2 x 3 — re-read what the question is asking for.
You started the factor tree correctly, but 15 is not prime — it still splits into 3 × 5. Keep going until every branch ends in a prime.
This is a real factor pair of 30, but 10 is composite (10 = 2 × 5). A prime factorization can only contain prime factors.
hints: A prime factorization uses ONLY prime numbers. Look at each choice: are ALL of its factors prime?
Break 30 down step by step, and keep splitting any factor that is still composite until every factor is prime.
Start with 30 = 2 × 15. Is 15 prime? No — so split 15 into two primes and collect everything you found.
approaching.explanationEs: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. Los tres factores (2, 3 y 5) son primos, por eso 2 × 3 × 5 es la factorización prima.
hintsEs: Una factorización prima usa SOLO números primos. Mira cada opción: ¿son primos TODOS sus factores?
Descompón el 30 paso a paso y sigue partiendo cualquier factor que todavía sea compuesto hasta que todos los factores sean primos.
Empieza con 30 = 2 × 15. ¿Es primo el 15? No — así que parte el 15 en dos primos y reúne todo lo que encontraste.

approaching.stem: What is the prime factorization of 18?
approaching.explanation: 18 = 2 × 9 = 2 × 3 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so 2 × 3 × 3 is the prime factorization.
choiceFeedback: That is what you get if you stopped too early — 9 is not prime, it still breaks down into 3 x 3 — re-read what the question is asking for.
3 is prime, but 6 is not — it still splits into 2 × 3. Keep breaking down the composite factor.
Changing the order does not fix the problem: 6 is still composite (6 = 2 × 3). Every factor in the final answer must be prime.
hints: Check every factor in each choice — numbers like 9 and 6 are composite, so they can't appear in a prime factorization.
Build a factor tree for 18: split it into two factors, then keep splitting anything composite until only primes remain.
Begin with 18 = 2 × 9. The 9 isn't prime, so break 9 into two equal prime factors and list all the primes you end with.
approaching.explanationEs: 18 = 2 × 9 = 2 × 3 × 3. Tanto 2 como 3 son primos, por eso 2 × 3 × 3 es la factorización prima.
hintsEs: Revisa cada factor de cada opción — números como el 9 y el 6 son compuestos, así que no pueden aparecer en una factorización prima.
Arma un árbol de factores para el 18: pártelo en dos factores y sigue partiendo lo compuesto hasta que solo queden primos.
Comienza con 18 = 2 × 9. El 9 no es primo, así que parte el 9 en dos factores primos iguales y escribe todos los primos con los que terminas.

approaching.stem: Which of these numbers is composite?
approaching.explanation: 27 = 3 × 9 = 3 × 3 × 3, so it has more than two factors. 23, 29, and 31 are all prime.
choiceFeedback: 23 is prime — dividing by 2, 3, or 5 always leaves a remainder. A composite number must break into smaller factors.
29 has no factor pair other than 1 × 29 — dividing by 2, 3, and 5 always leaves a remainder. A composite number has a factor pair you can actually find.
31 cannot be written as a product of two smaller whole numbers greater than 1. Test each number for a factor pair before you choose.
hints: Composite means MORE than two factors. Ask for each number: can I split it into two smaller whole numbers?
Try dividing each choice by small primes like 2, 3, and 5. A digit-sum divisible by 3 means the whole number divides by 3.
Test 23 first: try 2, 3, and 5 — none divide it evenly, so 23 is prime. Cross it off and test the other numbers the same way.
approaching.explanationEs: 27 = 3 × 9 = 3 × 3 × 3, así que tiene más de dos factores. 23, 29 y 31 son todos primos.
hintsEs: Compuesto significa MÁS de dos factores. Pregunta de cada número: ¿puedo separarlo en dos números enteros más pequeños?
Prueba dividir cada opción entre primos pequeños como 2, 3 y 5. Si la suma de los dígitos es divisible entre 3, todo el número es divisible entre 3.
Prueba primero el 23: intenta con 2, 3 y 5 — ninguno lo divide exactamente, así que 23 es primo. Táchalo y prueba los otros números de la misma manera.

approaching.title: Spot the Common Mistake

workedExample.label: Check each factor
workedExample.work: 5 is prime, so that branch is done.
workedExample.workEs: 5 es primo, así que esa rama está terminada.

approaching.correctWork: 4 is not prime because 4 = 2 × 2, so the tree needs one more split. The complete prime factorization is 20 = 2 × 2 × 5.
hints: Look at every factor in the final answer — is each one a prime number?
4 is composite because 4 = 2 × 2, so 4 still needs to be broken apart.
approaching.explanation: The factor tree stopped one split too early. The check tested only the 5 and left the 4 alone, but 4 = 2 × 2 is composite, so 20 = 4 × 5 is not a prime factorization. Splitting that 4 gives the complete answer, 20 = 2 × 2 × 5.
approaching.explanationEs: El árbol de factores se detuvo una división antes de tiempo. La revisión solo probó el 5 y dejó el 4 sin tocar, pero 4 = 2 × 2 es compuesto, así que 20 = 4 × 5 no es una factorización prima. Al dividir ese 4 se obtiene la respuesta completa: 20 = 2 × 2 × 5.
approaching.correctWorkEs: 4 no es primo porque 4 = 2 × 2, así que el árbol necesita una división más. La factorización prima completa es 20 = 2 × 2 × 5.
hintsEs: Mira cada factor de la respuesta final — ¿cada uno es un número primo?
4 es compuesto porque 4 = 2 × 2, así que todavía hay que descomponer el 4.

approaching.stem: Two students found different factor trees for 60. Student A started with 2 × 30. Student B started with 6 × 10. Which statement is true?
choices: Both get the same prime factorization: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5
Only Student A gets the correct prime factorization
Only Student B gets the correct prime factorization
They will get different prime factorizations
approaching.explanation: The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every composite number has exactly one prime factorization. No matter how you start the factor tree, you always end with 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
choiceFeedback: Not quite. The Fundamental Theorem of Arithmetic says every composite number has exactly one prime factorization.
Starting with 6 × 10 is allowed, but so is starting with 2 × 30 — the opening pair does not decide who is right. Finish both trees and compare the primes at the ends.
Different starting pairs make the trees look different, but the primes at the very ends are what count. Finish both trees and list those primes before deciding.
hints: Notice the question isn't asking which START is right — it asks what happens when both finished trees are compared.
Finish BOTH trees yourself: keep splitting every branch down to primes, then compare the two final lists of prime factors.
Student A: 60 = 2 × 30, then 30 = 2 × 15, then 15 = 3 × 5. Now finish Student B's tree from 6 × 10 and compare the prime lists.
approaching.stemEs: Dos estudiantes hicieron árboles de factores diferentes para 60. El estudiante A empezó con 2 × 30. El estudiante B empezó con 6 × 10. ¿Cuál afirmación es verdadera?
approaching.explanationEs: El Teorema Fundamental de la Aritmética dice que todo número compuesto tiene exactamente una factorización prima. No importa cómo empieces el árbol de factores, siempre terminas con 2 × 2 × 3 × 5.
choicesEs: Los dos obtienen la misma factorización prima: 2 × 2 × 3 × 5
Solo el Estudiante A obtiene la factorización prima correcta
Solo el Estudiante B obtiene la factorización prima correcta
hintsEs: Fíjate que la pregunta no pregunta cuál INICIO es correcto — pregunta qué pasa cuando se comparan los dos árboles terminados.
Termina TÚ los DOS árboles: sigue partiendo cada rama hasta llegar a primos y luego compara las dos listas finales de factores primos.
Estudiante A: 60 = 2 × 30, luego 30 = 2 × 15, luego 15 = 3 × 5. Ahora termina el árbol del Estudiante B desde 6 × 10 y compara las listas de primos.

onLevel.stem: The first lock panel shows 90. What is the prime factorization of 90?
onLevel.explanation: 90 = 2 × 45 = 2 × 9 × 5 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. Every factor is prime, so the lock accepts 2 × 3 × 3 × 5.
choiceFeedback: That is what you get if you stopped too early — 45 is not prime — keep splitting until every factor is prime: 45 = 3 × 3 × 5 — re-read what the question is asking for.
Both 9 and 10 are composite, so this is a factor pair rather than a prime factorization. Each one still needs to be split.
3 is prime, but 30 is not — it still breaks into 2 × 3 × 5. Keep splitting until nothing composite is left.
onLevel.stemEs: El primer panel del candado muestra 90. ¿Cuál es la factorización prima de 90?
onLevel.explanationEs: 90 = 2 × 45 = 2 × 9 × 5 = 2 × 3 × 3 × 5. Todos los factores son primos, por eso el candado acepta 2 × 3 × 3 × 5.
hints: A prime factorization lists only prime numbers — numbers with exactly two factors, like 2, 3, 5, 7, 11, and 13.
Build a factor tree: split 90 into any factor pair, then keep splitting any factor that is not prime.
Start with 90 = 2 × 45. The 2 is prime, but 45 is not — split 45 into a factor pair and keep going until every branch is prime.
hintsEs: Una factorización prima solo contiene números primos: números con exactamente dos factores, como 2, 3, 5, 7, 11 y 13.
Haz un árbol de factores: divide 90 en cualquier pareja de factores y sigue dividiendo los factores que no sean primos.
Empieza con 90 = 2 × 45. El 2 ya es primo, pero 45 no lo es: divide 45 en una pareja de factores y continúa hasta que todas las ramas sean primas.

onLevel.stem: The second panel needs a number whose prime factorization is 2² × 3². Which number unlocks it?
onLevel.explanation: 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36, so 36 is the code for this panel.
choiceFeedback: 24 breaks down as 2³ × 3 — that's three 2s but only one 3. Multiply out 2² × 3² (that's 4 × 9) and see which number it builds.
12 = 2 × 2 × 3, so it carries only one factor of 3. Count how many 3s the exponent is asking for.
18 = 2 × 3 × 3, which has only one factor of 2. Check the exponent on the 2 as well as the one on the 3.
onLevel.stemEs: El segundo panel necesita un número cuya factorización prima sea 2² × 3². ¿Cuál número lo desbloquea?
onLevel.explanationEs: 2² × 3² = 4 × 9 = 36, así que 36 es el código de este panel.
hints: An exponent tells you how many times a prime is used as a factor, so 2² means 2 × 2.
Write the expression out in full as a product of primes, then multiply to find the number.
2² × 3² becomes 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Multiply 2 × 2 = 4 first, then multiply that result by 3 × 3.
hintsEs: Un exponente indica cuántas veces se usa un primo como factor, así que 2² significa 2 × 2.
Escribe la expresión completa como un producto de primos y luego multiplica para hallar el número.
2² × 3² se convierte en 2 × 2 × 3 × 3. Multiplica primero 2 × 2 = 4 y luego multiplica ese resultado por 3 × 3.

onLevel.stem: The final lock asks for the prime factorization of 78 written as a product of primes. Which is correct?
onLevel.explanation: 78 = 2 × 39 = 2 × 3 × 13. All three factors are prime, so 2 × 3 × 13 unlocks the final panel.
choiceFeedback: That is what you get if you stopped too early — 39 is not prime, it still breaks down into 3 x 13 — re-read what the question is asking for.
3 is prime, but 26 is not — it splits into 2 × 13. Keep breaking down the composite factor.
13 is prime, but 6 is not (6 = 2 × 3). Every factor in the final product has to be prime.
onLevel.stemEs: El candado final pide la factorización prima de 78 escrita como un producto de primos. ¿Cuál es la correcta?
onLevel.explanationEs: 78 = 2 × 39 = 2 × 3 × 13. Los tres factores son primos, por eso 2 × 3 × 13 abre el panel final.
hints: The answer must be a product of primes only — no composite numbers are allowed in the list.
78 is even, so start by pulling out a factor of 2, then keep factoring whatever is left.
78 = 2 × 39. Now check 39: it is not prime, so find its factor pair and finish the tree.
hintsEs: La respuesta debe ser un producto solo de primos: no se permiten números compuestos en la lista.
78 es par, así que empieza sacando un factor de 2 y sigue factorizando lo que queda.
78 = 2 × 39. Ahora revisa el 39: no es primo, así que busca su pareja de factores y termina el árbol.

onLevel.title: Level 2 Extension — Fix the Broken Factor Tree
onLevel.correctWork: 12 = 2 × 6, but 6 is not prime. 6 = 2 × 3, so 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. The complete prime factorization is 96 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁵ × 3.
hints: Check every factor in the final answer — is 6 a prime number?
6 is composite because 6 = 2 × 3, so the tree must keep splitting until every branch is prime.
onLevel.titleEs: Extensión de Nivel 2: Arregla el árbol de factores dañado
onLevel.explanation: The 12 branch stopped while 6 was still composite: 6 = 2 × 3, so 12 = 2 × 2 × 3, not 2 × 6. Finishing that branch gives 96 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁵ × 3.
onLevel.explanationEs: La rama del 12 se detuvo cuando el 6 todavía era compuesto: 6 = 2 × 3, así que 12 = 2 × 2 × 3, no 2 × 6. Al terminar esa rama se obtiene 96 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁵ × 3.
onLevel.correctWorkEs: 12 = 2 × 6, pero 6 no es primo. 6 = 2 × 3, así que 12 = 2 × 2 × 3. La factorización prima completa es 96 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁵ × 3.
hintsEs: Revisa cada factor de la respuesta final — ¿6 es un número primo?
6 es compuesto porque 6 = 2 × 3, así que el árbol debe seguir dividiéndose hasta que cada rama sea prima.

onLevel.title: Find Marcus's Mistake
onLevel.correctWork: 8 = 2 × 4, but 4 is not prime. 4 = 2 × 2, so 8 = 2 × 2 × 2. The correct prime factorization is 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁴ × 3.
hints: Look at Step 4 — is every factor in the answer a prime number?
4 is not prime because 4 = 2 × 2. Marcus needed to keep breaking it down.
onLevel.explanation: Marcus stopped the 8 branch while a composite factor was still in it: 4 is not prime because 4 = 2 × 2, so 8 = 2 × 2 × 2, not 2 × 4. Finishing that branch gives 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁴ × 3.
onLevel.explanationEs: Marcus detuvo la rama del 8 cuando todavía tenía un factor compuesto: 4 no es primo porque 4 = 2 × 2, así que 8 = 2 × 2 × 2, no 2 × 4. Al terminar esa rama se obtiene 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁴ × 3.
onLevel.correctWorkEs: 8 = 2 × 4, pero 4 no es primo. 4 = 2 × 2, así que 8 = 2 × 2 × 2. La factorización prima correcta es 48 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 = 2⁴ × 3.
hintsEs: Mira el Paso 4 — ¿cada factor de la respuesta es un número primo?
4 no es primo porque 4 = 2 × 2. Marcus tenía que seguir descomponiéndolo.

onLevel.prompt: Choose any two-digit composite number. Show TWO different factor trees that both lead to the same prime factorization. Explain why every composite number has only one prime factorization.
onLevel.sentenceFrame: I chose the number ___. My first factor tree starts with ___ × ___, and my second starts with ___ × ___. Both give the same prime factorization: ___. This happens because ___.
hints: Re-read the task: pick ONE two-digit composite number (like 24, 36, or 40) and build TWO trees with different first splits.
Choose two different starting pairs for your number — for 36 you could start with 4 × 9 or 6 × 6 — and finish both trees to primes.
Say you pick 24: tree one starts 2 × 12, tree two starts 4 × 6. Finish both, list each tree's primes, and explain why the lists match.
onLevel.explanation: A strong answer picks one two-digit composite number and finishes two trees that begin with different first splits — for 24, starting with 2 × 12 and starting with 4 × 6 both end at 2 × 2 × 2 × 3. The lists always match because splitting only pulls composite factors apart into primes that were already inside the number, so the set of primes cannot change.
onLevel.explanationEs: Una buena respuesta elige un número compuesto de dos dígitos y termina dos árboles que comienzan con divisiones distintas: para 24, empezar con 2 × 12 y empezar con 4 × 6 llevan los dos a 2 × 2 × 2 × 3. Las listas siempre coinciden porque dividir solo separa los factores compuestos en primos que ya estaban dentro del número, así que el conjunto de primos no puede cambiar.
onLevel.promptEs: Escoge cualquier número compuesto de dos dígitos. Muestra DOS árboles de factores diferentes que lleguen a la misma factorización prima. Explica por qué cada número compuesto tiene una sola factorización prima.
hintsEs: Relee la tarea: escoge UN número compuesto de dos dígitos (como 24, 36 o 40) y arma DOS árboles con primeras divisiones diferentes.
Elige dos parejas de inicio distintas para tu número — para 36 podrías empezar con 4 × 9 o con 6 × 6 — y termina los dos árboles hasta llegar a primos.
Digamos que escoges el 24: el primer árbol empieza con 2 × 12 y el segundo con 4 × 6. Termina los dos, escribe los primos de cada árbol y explica por qué las listas coinciden.

practice.commonMistake: A common mistake in Prime Factorization is stopping the factor tree too soon — leaving a composite number like 4, 6, 8, or 9 in the final answer instead of continuing to split it. For example, writing 20 = 4 × 5 as the prime factorization (4 is composite) instead of finishing with 20 = 2 × 2 × 5. Before you submit, check every number in your final answer: if any factor can still be broken into smaller factors, the tree isn't finished yet.

optionalActivity.name: Factor Tree Code Breaker
optionalActivity.intro: Optional — one more together if the group is ready: The station's airlock is sealed with a prime-factor code — break each number into primes to unlock all four digits and reboard the ship!

connect.scenario: A station gardener is loading 72 seed pods into the greenhouse and wants to build a perfectly rectangular planting grid. Starting from the prime factorization of 72, she combines the prime factors to list every factor of 72 and choose a grid that uses all the pods.
connect.promptQuestion: Starting from its prime factorization, how can the gardener use the factors of 72 to decide which rectangular grids will use all 72 seed pods?
connect.prompt: Because 72 = ___, I can multiply combinations of those prime factors to get factors like ___, so a grid that works is ___ by ___.

check.stem: What is the prime factorization of 72?
check.explanation: 72 = 8 × 9 = (2 × 2 × 2) × (3 × 3) = 2³ × 3². 8 × 9 and 6 × 12 are factor pairs, but those numbers are not prime.

check.stem: The gardener wants a grid with 8 rows. How many pods in each row so all 72 are used?
check.explanation: 72 ÷ 8 = 9, so an 8-by-9 grid uses every pod.

check.stem: Which grid would NOT use exactly all 72 seed pods?
check.explanation: 5 × 14 = 70, not 72 — and 5 is not a factor of 72, since 2³ × 3² contains no 5. The other three grids all multiply to exactly 72.

connect.modelAnswer: 72 = 2 × 2 × 2 × 3 × 3 = 2³ × 3². Multiplying combinations of those primes gives every factor: 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 8, 9, 12, 18, 24, 36, 72. Each factor pair is a grid that uses all 72 pods — 6 by 12, 8 by 9, 4 by 18, and so on. A number like 5 or 7 never appears in the prime factorization, so a 5-row grid can never come out even.

exitTicket.stem: Quick check — you've got this: What is the prime factorization of 40?
exitTicket.hint: Think through the problem step by step.
choiceFeedback: 4 and 10 aren't prime — keep splitting until every factor is prime.
8 isn't prime — break it down further into primes.
20 still breaks down — a prime factorization stops only at primes.
hints: A prime factorization keeps going until EVERY factor is prime — factors like 4, 8, 10, and 20 still need splitting.
Build a factor tree for 40 and keep splitting every composite branch until only prime numbers are left at the ends.
Start with 40 = 4 × 10. Split the 4 into 2 × 2, then split the 10 into primes — then collect every prime at the ends of the branches.

questions.stem: Which of these numbers is composite?
questions.explanation: 27 = 3 × 9 = 3 × 3 × 3, so it has more than two factors. 23, 29, and 31 are all prime.

questions.stem: Which of the following is a prime number?
questions.explanation: 17 has exactly two factors: 1 and 17. 15 = 3 × 5, 21 = 3 × 7, and 9 = 3 × 3, so they are all composite.

questions.stem: What is the prime factorization of 18?
questions.explanation: 18 = 2 × 9 = 2 × 3 × 3. Both 2 and 3 are prime, so 2 × 3 × 3 is the prime factorization.

questions.stem: What is the prime factorization of 30?
questions.explanation: 30 = 2 × 15 = 2 × 3 × 5. All three factors (2, 3, 5) are prime, so 2 × 3 × 5 is the prime factorization.
